t: 3256. Maximum Value Sum by Placing Three Rooks I
o: Place three non-attacking rooks (pairwise distinct rows and columns) on an m x n board to maximize the sum of covered cell values; values may be negative. With m, n <= 100, checking all cell triples is impossible, but the key observation is that any valid placement uses exactly 3 rows and 3 columns. Enumerating row triples (at most C(100,3) ≈ 161700) and solving the resulting 3-row, n-column assignment with a tiny column-sweep bitmask DP is fast enough.
k: Fix the set of 3 rows first; then the problem reduces to picking 3 distinct columns and assigning rows to them.
A DP over columns with an 8-state row mask solves the 3 x n assignment in O(n · 8 · 3).
Transposing so the triple is taken over the smaller dimension minimizes C(dim, 3) work.

a.n: Approach 1: Row-Triple Enumeration + Column Mask DP
a.i: Every answer uses some triple of rows. For a fixed triple, sweep columns left to right keeping dp[mask] = best sum placing rooks (according to the bits of mask) in distinct columns seen so far. Each column offers at most one cell per row; transitions either skip the column or place one rook in a free row. dp[full] after the sweep is the best placement for that row triple; the global maximum over triples is the answer. Transposing when m > n keeps the triple count minimal.
s: If m > n, transpose the board so rows are the smaller dimension.
For each row triple (i, j, k), initialize dp[0] = 0 and dp[other] = -infinity.
For each column, copy dp and try placing a rook for each unset row bit using that column's value.
Update the global answer with dp[7] after the sweep.
a.t: O(C(min(m,n), 3) · max(m,n) · 8) ≈ 1.3e8 elementary steps at the limits — fast in compiled languages, tight but workable in Python
a.sp: O(max(m,n)) per triple for the DP array (plus O(nm) if transposing)

w: The transposition step is an easy constant-factor win — always enumerate triples over the smaller dimension. Beware negative values: initialize with true negative infinity, not 0, and never let 'skip' transitions pollute unfilled masks. A follow-up asks for k rooks generally (LC 3259): the same idea extends with a 2^k mask, feasible for small k; for large k one needs min-cost matching or Hungarian-style algorithms.
